html:
The "Law of the Kings", a code of church and civil law used in Ethiopia for about five hundred years. It began as an Arabic work compiled in the 13th century by the Egyptian Coptic scholar al-Safi ibn al-Assal for the Coptic Church, drawing on the Bible, church councils and Roman law.

It was translated into Ge'ez around 1450, by tradition in the reign of Zara Yaqob. The first part covers the clergy, sacraments and fasting; the second covers family, property, crime and the duties of kings.

The Ethiopian Empire treated it as the highest law. Judges cited it alongside custom until Haile Selassie brought in a written constitution in 1931 and modern codes in the decades after. With the Kebra Nagast, it is one of the books that shaped how the Ethiopian state saw itself.
